questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Vector Equation of the Plane Perpendicular to a Given Vector
questions.problem: Find an equation of the plane that contains the point $P(2,-5,3)$ and is perpendicular to the vector $n=⟨-1,2,-3⟩.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that the position vector of $P$ is $p=⟨2,-5,3⟩,$ and $n=⟨-1,2,-3⟩$ is normal to the plane.

The equation of the plane that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is perpendicular to the vector $n$ can be given as

$$
(r-p)\cdot n=0,
$$

where $r$ is the position vector of any point on the plane, and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨-1,2,-3⟩ & =⟨2,-5,3⟩\cdot ⟨-1,2,-3⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨-1,2,-3⟩ & =-21.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Vector That Is Parallel To a Plane
questions.problem: A nonzero vector $⟨a,\,b,\,0⟩$ is parallel to the plane $r\cdot ⟨6,-2,0⟩=-14.$ What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We need a vector $v=⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩$ that is parallel to the given plane. 

From the equation $r\cdot ⟨6,-2,0⟩=-14$ of the plane, we get the normal vector $n=⟨6,-2,0⟩.$ So, $v⊥n$ and we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}v\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨6,-2,0⟩ & =0 \\ 6{t}_{1}-2{t}_{2} & =0 \\ {t}_{2} & =3{t}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we obtain 

$$
v=⟨{t}_{1},3{t}_{1},{t}_{3}⟩,
$$

where ${t}_{1},{t}_{3}\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ 

We are told that the third component of $v$ eqauls $0.$ So, we must set ${t}_{3}=0.$ 

Since $v$ is nonzero, we can pick any ${t}_{1}\ne 0.$ For example, setting ${t}_{1}=1$, we get

$$
v=⟨1,\,3,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{1}{3}.$

questions.problem: A nonzero vector $⟨a,\,0,\,c⟩$ is parallel to the plane $r\cdot ⟨-1,2,2⟩=\sqrt{11}.$ What is the value of $\frac{a}{c}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We need a vector $v=⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩$ that is parallel to the given plane. 

From the equation $r\cdot ⟨-1,2,2⟩=\sqrt{11}$ of the plane, we get the normal vector $n=⟨-1,2,2⟩.$ So, $v⊥n$ and we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}v\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨-1,2,2⟩ & =0 \\ -{t}_{1}+2{t}_{2}+2{t}_{3} & =0 \\ {t}_{1} & =2{t}_{2}+2{t}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we obtain 

$$
v=⟨2{t}_{2}+2{t}_{3},\,{t}_{2},\,{t}_{3}⟩,
$$

where ${t}_{2},{t}_{3}\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ 

We are told that the second component of $v$ equals $0.$ So, we must set ${t}_{2}=0.$ 

Since $v$ is nonzero, we can pick any ${t}_{3}\ne 0.$ For example, setting ${t}_{3}=1$, we get

$$
v=⟨2,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Therefore, $\frac{a}{c}=2.$

From the equation $r\cdot ⟨-3,1,-2⟩=7$ of the plane, we get the normal vector $n=⟨-3,1,-2⟩.$ So, $v⊥n$ and we have the following:

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Vector Equation of the Plane Perpendicular to a Given Straight Line
questions.problem:
Find an equation of the plane that passes through the point $Q(2,1,-3)$ and is  perpendicular to the line 

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=1+t \\ y=2-t \\ z=3+2t.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Note that the position vector of $Q$ is $q=⟨2,1,-3⟩.$ Converting the parametric equations of the line to vector form, we get

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=1+t \\ y=2-t \\ z=3+2t\end{aligned}\,⇒\,⟨x,y,z⟩=⟨1,2,3⟩+t\text{ }{{⟨1,-1,2⟩}_{⏟}}_{v}.
$$

   

The direction vector of the line is $v=⟨1,-1,2⟩.$ So, a normal  vector to the plane is 

$$
n=v=⟨1,-1,2⟩.
$$

 

Therefore, the equation of the plane is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-q)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n-q\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =q\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨1,-1,2⟩ & =⟨2,1,-3⟩\cdot ⟨1,-1,2⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨1,-1,2⟩ & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find an equation of the plane that passes through the point $Q(2,1,-1)$ and is perpendicular to the line that goes through the points 
$A(2,1,0)$ and $B(3,2,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that the position vector of $Q$ is $q=⟨2,1,-1⟩.$

Since the line  passes through the points $A(2,1,0)$ and $B(3,2,1)$ we can find a vector parallel to the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨3,2,1⟩-⟨2,1,0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, a normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨1,1,1⟩.$ 

Therefore, the equation of the plane is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-q)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n-q\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =q\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨1,1,1⟩ & =⟨2,1,-1⟩\cdot ⟨1,1,1⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨1,1,1⟩ & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find an equation of the plane that contains the point $P(-3,2,1)$ and is perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf{n}= \langle 0, 2, 0 \rangle.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we note that the position vector of $P$ is $\mathbf{p}=\langle -3,2,1 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{n}=\langle 0,2,0 \rangle$ is normal to the plane.

The equation of the plane that passes through the point $P(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ and is perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf{n}$ can be given as

$$
(\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{p}) \cdot \mathbf{n} = 0,
$$

where $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector of any point on the plane, and $\mathbf p$ is the position vector of $P.$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨0,2,0⟩ & =⟨-3,2,1⟩\cdot ⟨0,2,0⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨0,2,0⟩ & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: A nonzero vector $\langle 0,\, \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{b}, \: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{c} \rangle$ is parallel to the plane $\mathbf{r} \cdot \langle 2, -1, 4 \rangle  = 3.$ What is the value of $\dfrac{b}{c}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We need a vector $\mathbf{v} = \langle t_1,t_2,t_3 \rangle$ that is parallel to the given plane. 

From the equation $\mathbf{r} \cdot \langle 2, -1, 4 \rangle  = 3$ of the plane, we get the normal vector $\mathbf{n}=\langle 2, -1, 4 \rangle.$ So, $\mathbf{v} \perp \mathbf{n}$ and we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}v\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨2,-1,4⟩ & =0 \\ 2{t}_{1}-{t}_{2}+4{t}_{3} & =0 \\ {t}_{2} & =2{t}_{1}+4{t}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we obtain 

$$
\mathbf{v}=\langle t_1, 2t_1 + 4t_3, t_3 \rangle,
$$

where $t_1,t_3 \in (-\infty,\infty).$ 

We are told that the first component of $\mathbf{v}$ equals $0.$ So, we must set $t_1=0.$ 

Since $\mathbf{v}$ is nonzero, we can pick any $t_3 \neq 0.$ For example, setting $t_3=1$, we get

$$
\mathbf{v} = \langle 0,\, \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{4}, \, \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{1} \rangle.
$$

Therefore, $\dfrac{b}{c} = 4.$

Therefore, the equation of the plane is given by

$$
